title: Crypto & Speculation
description: Tokens, scams, and the small slice you can actually lose.
wolfLine: A story is not a plan. The fee to unlock your money is a scam.

cryptocurrency.definition: A digital token recorded on a shared ledger. Its price is what the next buyer will pay. It pays no coupon and it can go to zero.
cryptocurrency.example: A coin that was $1,000 and is later $400.

lessons.title: What Crypto Is
lessons.summary: A token with a price, not a plan.

steps.title: No coupon, no building
steps.body: A [[cryptocurrency]] is a digital token on a shared ledger. Nobody owes you interest. There is no company earnings line and no rent. The price is the next buyer. This unit is education. It is not a coin to buy, and it will not name one.

steps.prompt: What sets a coin’s price?
choices: A coupon written on the token
Whatever the next buyer will pay
steps.explain: No coupon, no insurance on the price. Buyers and sellers are the whole price.

steps.prompt: A cryptocurrency pays a bond-style coupon.
steps.explain: There is no issuer promising interest and a face value back. The price can go to zero.

steps.prompt: How should you read this unit?
choices: As a list of coins to buy
As education about a risky token, not a recommendation
As a replacement for an index fund
steps.explain: No ticker. No promise. The risks are the lesson.

steps.prompt: A digital token whose price is the next buyer is a ___.
steps.explain: Cryptocurrency. A CD is a bank deposit. A coupon is a bond’s interest.

lessons.title: A 60% Drop
lessons.summary: The math does not care about the story.

steps.title: Round and harsh
steps.body: Crypto prices have swung harder than a broad stock [[index]]. This lesson uses one clean case: a $1,000 coin falls 60%. You have $400. The other $600 is gone unless the price comes back, which it does not owe you. Historically, on average, is the wrong phrase here. A single coin is not “the market.”

steps.prompt: A $1,000 coin falls 60%. How many dollars are left?
How many dollars did that drop destroy?
A 60% drop needs only a 60% rise to get back to $1,000.
What percent gain turns $400 back into $1,000?
steps.explain: You need $600 more on a $400 base. $600 ÷ $400 = 1.50, which is 150%.

lessons.title: Scams and Rug Pulls
lessons.summary: The fee to unlock your money is the tell.

steps.title: Two shapes
steps.body: A rug pull is when the people behind a new token take the money and disappear. The other shape is a message: your coins are “up,” but you must send a fee before you can withdraw. Real investments do not charge you a secret fee to touch your own money. Nobody legitimate needs you to move coins to a stranger’s wallet so they can “fix” an account.

doc.title: A message, not a market
doc.subtitle: You cannot withdraw until you pay

lines.label: Unlock fee they want sent first

doc.note: A fee to unlock your own money is the scam.

steps.prompt: Which line is the scam?
steps.explain: The $80 unlock fee is the trap. The $2,000 “gain” is the bait. You do not pay a stranger to access your own money.

steps.prompt: A promise of 10% every day is a normal yield.
steps.explain: Ten percent a day is the shape of a scam, not a bond yield. Walk away.

steps.prompt: Someone asks you to send coins to a wallet they control so they can repair your account. What do you do?
choices: Stop. Do not send anything. Real support does not need your coins moved to them.
Send more, because the gain looks large
steps.explain: Moving the coins to them is the theft. Stop.

steps.prompt: The bait says you are up $2,000, and the unlock fee is $80. If you pay it and the “gain” was never real, how many dollars did you just hand over?
steps.explain: The $80 is gone. The $2,000 was a picture on a screen.

lessons.title: Exchanges and Custody
lessons.summary: Someone else holding it is a risk of its own.

steps.title: Who has the coins
steps.body: On an exchange, the platform holds the coins and you have an account. If the platform freezes withdrawals or fails, you are in line with everyone else. A private wallet puts the keys with you. Lose the keys and the coins are gone. There is no password reset. Do not assume [[SIPC]] covers a crypto app. SIPC is about securities at member brokerages, not about a coin’s price, and not about a typical crypto platform.

steps.prompt: You keep coins on an exchange. Who is holding them?
choices: Your bank, with FDIC insurance on the coin’s price
steps.explain: The platform. If it fails or freezes, that is your problem. The coin’s price is a separate risk.

steps.prompt: SIPC replaces a drop in a coin’s price.
steps.explain: SIPC does not cover a market drop, and a typical crypto app is not that kind of brokerage protection anyway.

steps.prompt: You hold the keys in a private wallet and you lose them. What happens?
steps.explain: No reset. The keys are the ownership. This is why “I’ll remember it” is not a plan, and why a coin is a bad place for rent money.

steps.prompt: If the platform holds the coins for you, that platform is the ___.
steps.explain: Exchange. Your account is an IOU from them until you withdraw.

lessons.title: Speculation or Investing
lessons.summary: A plan has earnings or a coupon. A bet has a story.

steps.title: The line
steps.body: [[Investing]], in this course, means owning a broad fund, a bond, or a real business you can leave alone for years. Speculation is a bet that a price will rise because other people will pay more. A coin, a meme stock, and a short-term options bet sit on the speculation side. You may still do it. You do not call it the plan.

steps.prompt: Which pile is this?
items: A broad index fund for a 30-year goal
A coin bought because a video said it would triple
A Treasury you intend to hold to maturity
A meme stock from a screenshot
steps.explain: The plan has a job and a long date. The screenshot and the video are bets that someone else pays more.

steps.prompt: Calling a bet an investment changes what it is.
steps.explain: The name does not add earnings, a coupon, or a recovery schedule.

steps.prompt: Where does a coin you cannot explain sit?
choices: On the speculation side, in money you can lose
Inside the 401(k) match, as the whole match
steps.explain: If you do it, it is a slice you can lose. It is not the rent, the match, or the emergency fund.

steps.prompt: A bet that someone else will pay more is ___.
steps.explain: Speculation. The plan is the fund, the bond, and the years.

lessons.title: How Much Is Too Much
lessons.summary: Rent money is too much. A slice you can lose is the cap.

steps.title: The test
steps.body: The cap is the amount you can watch go to zero without missing rent, food, or the [[emergency fund]]. If that amount is $200, then $200 is the cap. A $2,000 buy is $1,800 past it. There is no clever percent that makes a coin safe. The test is the bills.

steps.prompt: You can afford to lose $200. You are about to buy $2,000 of a coin. How many dollars over the cap is that?
Five percent of your money is a safe rule that makes a coin fine.
steps.explain: No percent makes the price safe. The test is whether you can lose the dollars and still pay your life.

steps.prompt: Which pile is allowed to be the speculation slice?
choices: Money you can lose without missing a bill
steps.explain: Loseable money only. The emergency fund and the rent have jobs.

steps.prompt: Your cap is $200 and you already bought $200 of a coin. How many more dollars fit inside the cap?
steps.explain: The cap is full. More would be money you decided you could not lose.

lessons.title: Meme Stocks and Options
lessons.summary: A bet can expire. The plan should not.

steps.title: Same family as the coin
steps.body: A meme stock is a share people pile into because it is a story, not because you read the business. An option is a contract with a deadline. The premium you pay can expire and be worth $0. A $300 option can become nothing. Neither belongs in the emergency fund, the match, or the long-term [[index fund]]. If you touch them, they are speculation, in the small slice.

steps.prompt: You pay a $300 option premium and it expires worthless. How many dollars are left of that premium?
steps.explain: Worthless means $0. The $300 is the cost of the bet, gone.

steps.prompt: A meme stock is a diversified index fund with a fun name.
steps.explain: It is one company, plus a crowd. One company is concentration. The crowd is not a plan.

steps.prompt: Where do options and meme stocks belong in this course’s sorting?
choices: The core of the retirement mix
With speculation, in money you can lose
Inside the emergency fund, because they are exciting
steps.explain: The slice you can lose. The retirement mix stays the broad, cheap funds.

steps.prompt: What can an option do that a savings account cannot?
choices: Get FDIC insurance on the premium
steps.explain: The deadline is the point. The premium can vanish. Savings do not expire.

lessons.title: Kai’s Lesson
lessons.summary: The drop was real. The “agent” was the second trap.

story.title: The video and the agent
story.body:
Kai put **$1,000** into a coin. It fell **60%**, to **$400**. A “support agent” then asked for **$200** to unlock the account.

He did not send it. His Roth IRA index fund stayed where it was.

steps.title: Meet Kai
steps.body:
Kai is 24 and a barista. He put $1,000 into a coin after a video. It fell 60%, to $400. Then a “support agent” offered to unlock the loss if Kai sent $200 first.

He did not send it. His real plan, a broad index fund in his Roth IRA, was untouched. Any future bet stays inside $100 he can lose.

steps.prompt: How many dollars did Kai lose on the 60% drop?
steps.explain: $1,000 − $400 = $600. The video did not change the subtraction.

steps.prompt: If he had paid the unlock fee, how many more dollars would have left, on top of the $600?
steps.explain: The $200 would be a second loss. The agent does not have his coins to unlock.

steps.prompt: Kai should move his Roth IRA index fund into the coin to win the $600 back.
steps.explain: The fund is the plan. Chasing the loss with the plan is how a speculation becomes the whole portfolio.

steps.prompt: What did Kai get right?
choices: Refusing to send $200 to a stranger, and leaving the index fund alone
Emptying the emergency fund to average down
steps.explain: The drop already happened. The scam was optional, and he skipped it. The fund stayed the plan.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Crypto & Speculation
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A $2,500 coin falls 60%. How many dollars are left?
You should send a fee to a stranger before you can withdraw.
steps.explain: A fee to unlock your own money is the scam. Do not send it.

steps.prompt: A meme stock belongs in which pile?
choices: Speculation, with money you can lose
The bond you hold to maturity
steps.explain: It is a bet on a crowd. The plan stays the broad fund and the real bills.

steps.prompt: Your loseable cap is $150 and a friend wants you to put in $500. How many dollars over the cap is $500?
